title: Petra and the Semester
premise: At Northgate High, the annual college essay contest is a formality — until this year's prompt, 'What has been taken from you?', unlocks something in every student who answers it honestly. Beatrix Ishikawa's essay about her mother's shuttered bakery accidentally names the school board member whose eminent-domain deal destroyed half the neighborhood, and when her draft leaks, the board moves to expel her before graduation. With help from three unlikely allies and a buried paper trail hidden in the school archive, Beatrix has eleven days to prove the corruption was systemic — and learns that justice won't come from the institutions meant to provide it. The book ends at the school board's final meeting, where Beatrix doesn't win the vote; she wins the room, forcing one board member to confess on record and the rest to resign rather than face what follows.
about_author: Ada Almeida grew up above her grandmother's bakery in a fading mill town, where she learned that recipes are just stories you can eat. She writes young adult fiction about quiet kids who refuse to stay quiet, and still judges people by how they treat cashiers.

chapters.title: The Crumb Rule
chapters.summary: Beatrix Ishikawa navigates Northgate High by strict invisibility: head down, grades up, locker shut. At home she bakes her unspoken feelings into bread her father sells without knowing their meaning. When English teacher Ms. Okafor announces the mandatory essay contest, Beatrix feels the first crack in her armor. POV: Beatrix. Beat: uneasy safety about to end.

chapters.title: One Honest Question
chapters.summary: The prompt is revealed: 'What has been taken from you?' The classroom goes silent; even the class cynic can't joke past it. Beatrix starts three safe drafts and abandons them all. That night she writes about her mother's bakery, closed by a city seizure order two years ago. POV: Beatrix. Beat: grief surfacing through flour and sugar.

chapters.title: What the Oven Remembers
chapters.summary: Beatrix submits the essay, then panics and begs Ms. Okafor to withdraw it. Okafor refuses gently: honest writing isn't a mistake. Meanwhile, other students' essays begin circulating — stolen lockers, deported siblings, a coach's abuse nobody reported. POV: Beatrix. Beat: dread mixed with the strange relief of being seen.

chapters.title: The Leak
chapters.summary: Beatrix's essay appears on the school gossip account, her name attached, quoting the seizure order signed by board chair Douglas Vann. By lunch, everyone knows. Her father reads it at the bakery counter and says nothing. POV: Beatrix. Beat: exposure as violation — and, underneath, a terrible freedom.

chapters.title: Vann's Smile
chapters.summary: Board chair Douglas Vann visits the school for a photo op, praising the essay contest while standing beside Beatrix like a trophy. His charm is flawless; his warning, delivered quietly, is not: 'Words have consequences, Miss Ishikawa.' POV: Beatrix. Beat: the mask of power shown up close.

chapters.title: Three Lockers Down
chapters.summary: Two unexpected allies appear: Theo Park, the gossip account's anonymous runner, and Marisol Vega, whose family lost their auto shop in the same seizure. They compare notes and find matching dates, matching signatures. POV: alternating Beatrix and Marisol. Beat: isolation breaking into conspiracy of the hopeful.

chapters.title: Detention Economics
chapters.summary: Retaliation begins subtly: Beatrix loses her scholarship recommendation, Marisol's work-study is cut, Theo gets suspended for an unrelated infraction. Ms. Okafor is reassigned to 'curriculum review.' POV: Beatrix. Beat: learning how power punishes without ever leaving fingerprints.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: Theo discovers the district keeps physical records in the school basement archive — including the original seizure hearings. The trio plans after-hours access during the winter concert. Beatrix hesitates; her father needs her steady, not expelled. POV: Beatrix. Beat: fear versus the arithmetic of what silence costs.

chapters.title: Bread for Thieves
chapters.summary: The night of the break-in. While the concert plays overhead, Beatrix photographs hearing transcripts revealing Vann bought seized properties through a shell company at ten cents on the dollar. A security guard nearly catches them; Marisol talks her way out. POV: Beatrix. Beat: adrenaline, guilt, and proof in hand.

chapters.title: Eleven Days
chapters.summary: The board schedules an emergency 'conduct hearing' for Beatrix — expulsion proceedings disguised as procedure. Graduation, scholarships, everything hangs on eleven days. Theo maps the deadline; Marisol lists witnesses. POV: Beatrix. Beat: the clock becomes a character.

chapters.title: Witness, Reluctant
chapters.summary: They approach former city clerk Ruth Delgado, who processed the filings and was pushed out afterward. She refuses at first — she has a pension, a life. Beatrix brings her bread baked from the old bakery's recipe, and Ruth's resolve cracks. POV: Beatrix. Beat: persuasion as inheritance, one recipe at a time.

chapters.title: The Turncoat Option
chapters.summary: A junior board member, Alan Reyes, privately signals he might testify if he's protected. The group debates trusting him; Theo argues no one inside the machine helps out of goodness. Beatrix chooses cautious trust. POV: Theo. Beat: hope weaponized against them, or so it seems.

chapters.title: Burnt Offering
chapters.summary: Reyes tips off Vann instead — or so it appears when the archive copies vanish from Theo's encrypted drive and the hearing moves up five days. The group fractures; Marisol accuses Beatrix of naivety. POV: Beatrix. Beat: betrayal, real or manufactured, at the lowest point.

chapters.title: Flour on Her Hands
chapters.summary: Alone, Beatrix almost signs a gag agreement Vann offers: full scholarship, sealed records, silence. She watches her father knead dough and realizes he never hid his anger — he just put it somewhere useful. She burns the agreement in the oven. POV: Beatrix. Beat: choosing the hard right over the easy wrong.

chapters.title: The Counter-Plan
chapters.summary: Reconciliation: Marisol reveals she kept duplicate photos off-site — she'd tested Beatrix's loyalty, harshly. Ruth Delgado agrees to testify publicly. Theo rebuilds the drive. They stop playing defense and plan to take over the hearing itself. POV: alternating all four. Beat: the team forged in fire.

chapters.title: Distributing the Loaves
chapters.summary: They print the evidence as a student zine and distribute five hundred copies before dawn — justice outside the law, delivered by hand. The school confiscates them; the internet does what the internet does. Local press calls. POV: Theo. Beat: the story escaping everyone's control, including theirs.

chapters.title: Hearing Day
chapters.summary: The conduct hearing convenes with Vann presiding over his own cover-up. Beatrix is questioned, stonewalled, condescended to. Then Ruth Delgado walks in uninvited with certified records, and Reyes, unexpectedly, stands up too. POV: Beatrix. Beat: the trap turning inside out.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Ruth testifies; the shell company unravels publicly. Vann tries to gavel it down, but parents in the gallery — customers of the bakery, clients of the auto shop — refuse to be silenced. One board member, cornered, confesses on the record. POV: Beatrix. Beat: climax; truth spoken aloud cannot be unspoken.

chapters.title: Aftermath Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Vann resigns rather than face investigation; two others follow. The expulsions are withdrawn, but nothing else is fixed — properties aren't returned, Okafor isn't reinstated yet. Beatrix learns winning doesn't restore what was taken. POV: Beatrix. Beat: bittersweet victory, honestly rendered.

chapters.title: The Essay Contest Results
chapters.summary: The contest results arrive: Beatrix doesn't win first place; the judges split the award among several essays, hers included. She realizes the prize was never the point. Ms. Okafor returns and tells her the essay will be taught next year. POV: Beatrix. Beat: recognition without coronation.

chapters.title: Reopening Day
chapters.summary: With settlement funds and community volunteers, the old bakery space reopens — not as her mother's shop, but as a shared kitchen and archive where the neighborhood's seized stories are collected. Beatrix bakes the first batch with her father. POV: Beatrix. Beat: inheritance reclaimed and transformed.

chapters.title: Next Year's Prompt
chapters.summary: Epilogue in spring: Beatrix, now a senior mentor, watches a new junior stare down the essay prompt with the same terror she felt. She slides a loaf of bread onto the kid's desk and says only, 'Tell the truth. We'll handle the rest.' POV: Beatrix. Beat: the cycle turned toward justice, passed on.
